**The Seagull**
Chekhov's 1896 play in which the young playwright Konstantin Treplev shoots a seagull and lays it at the feet of the aspiring actress Nina Zarechnaya, whom he loves. Nina instead falls for the established writer Boris Trigorin, the lover of Konstantin's mother, the actress Irina Arkadina. Later Nina compares herself to the seagull, and Konstantin shoots himself. It is the most commonly clued Chekhov work.

**Konstantin Treplev's suicide and Dr. Dorn's "medicine bottle"**
At the end of The Seagull, a gunshot is heard offstage. Dr. Dorn calmly tells the others that a bottle in his medicine case has burst, then quietly tells Trigorin that Konstantin has shot himself. Konstantin had already made one failed suicide attempt and appears with a bandaged head in Acts III and IV.

**The play-within-a-play in The Seagull**
Konstantin's symbolist play, performed by Nina, depicts the World Soul struggling against the devil, who is represented by two red eyes and the smell of sulfur. His mother Arkadina mocks it, and the performance stops abruptly. Dr. Dorn is the only one who praises it.

**"I'm in mourning for my life"**
Masha's reply in the opening lines of The Seagull when she is asked why she always wears black.

**The Cherry Orchard**
Chekhov's last play (1904). The indebted aristocrat Lyubov Ranevskaya and her brother Gayev, who is obsessed with billiards, lose their estate at auction to Lopakhin, a merchant whose father was a serf there. Ranevskaya returns to her lover in Paris at the end.

**Axes chopping and Firs left behind**
The Cherry Orchard ends with the offstage sound of axes cutting down the orchard. The elderly servant Firs is accidentally locked inside the abandoned house and lies down to die. The play also calls for the strange sound of a breaking string, "as if out of the sky."

**Chekhov's gun**
Chekhov's principle of dramatic economy: if a gun hangs on the wall in the first act, it must go off by the end of the play. Every element of a story should serve a purpose.

**Uncle Vanya**
In this play, Vanya (Ivan Voynitsky) has spent his life managing an estate to support his former brother-in-law, the retired professor Serebryakov, whom he later sees as a fraud and calls "a learned old dried mackerel." Vanya loves Serebryakov's young second wife Yelena, fires a pistol at Serebryakov twice and misses both times, and steals a bottle of morphine that Dr. Astrov makes him give back. The impoverished landowner Telegin is nicknamed "Waffles" because of his pockmarked face.

**Dr. Astrov and the forests**
The doctor in Uncle Vanya who gives passionate speeches about protecting Russia's forests from destruction. He is also attracted to Yelena.

**"The Lady with the Dog"**
A famous story in which Dmitri Gurov, a cynical married man who calls women "the lower race," has an affair in Yalta with Anna Sergeyevna, a young married woman walking a Pomeranian. He finds her again at an opening-night performance of The Geisha in her provincial town of S. The story ends with the realization that "the hardest, the most complicated part was only just beginning."

**Three Sisters**
A play about Olga, Masha, and Irina Prozorov, who long to return to Moscow from their provincial town. Masha is married to the schoolteacher Kulygin, and Baron Tuzenbach, engaged to the youngest sister Irina, is killed in a duel by Solyony. The drunken doctor Chebutykin breaks a porcelain clock and sings "Ta-ra-ra-boom-de-ay."

**"Ward No. 6"**
A novella in which Dr. Andrei Yefimich Ragin, who runs a provincial mental asylum, has philosophical conversations with the patient Ivan Dmitrich Gromov, including arguments about Stoicism. Ragin is then committed to his own ward, beaten by the guard Nikita, and dies of a stroke. Only the postmaster Mikhail Averyanovich and his cook attend his funeral.

**"The Bet"**
A story in which a banker bets two million rubles that a young lawyer cannot endure fifteen years of solitary confinement. The lawyer completes the term but renounces the money just before winning, having come to despise worldly things.

**Yalta**
The Crimean resort town where Chekhov lived in his last years because of his tuberculosis. He wrote The Cherry Orchard there, and it is the setting of "The Lady with the Dog."

**Other works: "The Black Monk," The Duel, Ivanov, "The Reed Pipe"**
In "The Black Monk," a scholar's vision of a ghostly monk tells him he is "one of God's chosen" and a genius. In the novella The Duel, the zoologist Von Koren nearly kills the idle Laevsky, who is living with a married woman. Ivanov is Chekhov's early play whose title character nearly marries Sasha Lebedeva. In "The Reed Pipe," a shepherd warns of the decline of nature.
